We present the first X-ray detection of the very young pulsar PSR J1357-6429 (characteristic age of 7.3 kyr) using data from the XMM-Newton and Chandra satellites. We find that the spectrum is well described by a power-law plus blackbody model, with photon index Gamma=1.4 and blackbody temperature kT=160 eV. For the estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, this corresponds to a 2-10 keV luminosity of about 1.2E+32 erg/s, thus the fraction of the spin-down energy channeled by PSR J1357-6429 into X-ray emission is one of the lowest observed. The Chandra data confirm the positional coincidence with the radio pulsar and allow to set an upper limit of 3E+31 erg/s on the 2-10 keV luminosity of a compact pulsar wind nebula. We do not detect any pulsed emission from the source and determine an upper limit of 30% for the modulation amplitude of the X-ray emission at the radio frequency of the pulsar.

# X-ray Detection of the Young Pulsar PSR J1357-6429

The very young pulsar PSR J1357-6429 has been detected in X-rays for the first time, using data obtained from the XMM-Newton and Chandra satellites. This marks an important milestone in the study of this pulsar, providing new insights into its high-energy emission properties.

## Spectral Characteristics

The X-ray spectrum of PSR J1357-6429 is well described by a composite model consisting of a power-law plus blackbody component. The power-law component is characterized by a photon index of 1.4, while the thermal blackbody component corresponds to a temperature of approximately 160 eV. This two-component model captures both the non-thermal emission, likely originating from the pulsar's magnetosphere, and the thermal emission arising from the heated neutron star surface.

## Luminosity and Energetics

Assuming an estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, the pulsar exhibits a 2-10 keV luminosity of approximately 1.2 × 10³² erg/s. Notably, this value represents one of the lowest fractions of spin-down energy channeled into X-ray emission ever observed for a pulsar of this class. This low conversion efficiency provides valuable constraints on the physical mechanisms responsible for high-energy emission in young neutron stars.

## Positional Confirmation and Pulsar Wind Nebula Constraints

The high angular resolution of the Chandra data confirmed the positional coincidence of the X-ray source with the previously identified radio source, firmly establishing the association. Furthermore, the Chandra observations placed a stringent upper limit of 3 × 10³¹ erg/s on the luminosity of any compact pulsar wind nebula that might surround the pulsar. This constraint is particularly significant given that young, energetic pulsars are often expected to power detectable wind nebulae.

## Search for Pulsed Emission

Despite a careful timing analysis, no pulsed X-ray emission was detected from PSR J1357-6429. This non-detection yielded an upper limit of 30% for the modulation amplitude at the pulsar's known radio frequency, further constraining the geometry and beaming properties of the pulsar's X-ray emission.

# X-ray Detection of the Young Pulsar PSR J1357-6429

## Introduction

PSR J1357-6429 is a very young rotation-powered pulsar with a characteristic age of approximately 7,300 years, making it one of the youngest neutron stars known in our Galaxy. Its youth and high spin-down energy make it an interesting target for studying the X-ray emission mechanisms of young pulsars and their interaction with the surrounding medium. In this work, we report the first detection of this pulsar in the X-ray band, using complementary observations obtained with the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories.

## Observations and Spectral Analysis

Our analysis combines the high sensitivity of XMM-Newton for spectral characterization with the superior angular resolution of Chandra, which is essential for identifying the point source associated with the pulsar and searching for any extended emission in its vicinity. The X-ray spectrum of PSR J1357-6429 is well described by a composite model consisting of a power-law component plus a blackbody component. This two-component spectral shape is commonly observed in young pulsars, where the power-law emission is attributed to non-thermal magnetospheric processes, while the blackbody component arises from thermal emission from the surface of the cooling neutron star or from localized heated regions such as the polar caps.

## Energetics and Efficiency

A remarkable property of PSR J1357-6429 is its exceptionally low efficiency in converting rotational energy into X-ray emission. We measure a luminosity in the 2-10 keV band of approximately 1.2 × 10³² erg/s. When compared to the pulsar's spin-down power, this corresponds to one of the lowest known fractions of spin-down energy channeled into X-ray radiation among rotation-powered pulsars. This low conversion efficiency provides important constraints on the emission mechanisms and the physical conditions in the pulsar magnetosphere.

## Search for Pulsations and a Pulsar Wind Nebula

Despite the clear detection of the source, we do not find evidence for pulsed emission from PSR J1357-6429 in the X-ray band; we place upper limits on the pulsed fraction based on the available timing data. Similarly, our high-resolution Chandra imaging reveals no compact pulsar wind nebula surrounding the pulsar down to the derived flux upper limits. The absence of a resolvable synchrotron nebula, combined with the low X-ray efficiency, may reflect the particular evolutionary stage or environmental conditions of this young neutron star.

## Conclusions

The first X-ray detection of PSR J1357-6429 adds a valuable object to the small sample of very young pulsars studied at high energies. Its combination of thermal and non-thermal spectral components, extremely low X-ray conversion efficiency, and the non-detection of both pulsations and a compact nebula make it a notable case for understanding the diversity of young pulsar properties. Future deeper observations with improved timing sensitivity and imaging capabilities will be needed to further characterize its emission and to clarify the nature of its interaction with the surrounding environment.

# Pulsars Through the Eyes of XMM-Newton

## Introduction

The study of neutron stars, particularly those observed as pulsars (designated by the prefix **PSR** in astronomical catalogs), represents one of the most exciting frontiers in modern astrophysics. Among the many instruments dedicated to unraveling the mysteries of these extreme objects, the **XMM-Newton** X-ray observatory has played a pivotal role in expanding our understanding of the high-energy universe.

## What Are Pulsars?

Pulsars, abbreviated as **PSR**, are highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles. As the star rotates, these beams sweep across space, and when they intersect with our line of sight, we detect regular pulses—much like the beam of a lighthouse. First discovered in 1967, pulsars are the compact remnants of massive stars that have undergone supernova explosions.

These objects are laboratories for extreme physics, exhibiting:

- **Incredible density** — cramming more than the mass of the Sun into a sphere roughly 20 kilometers across
- **Intense magnetic fields** — trillions of times stronger than Earth's
- **Precise rotation** — some spinning hundreds of times per second

## The XMM-Newton Observatory

The **X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission (XMM-Newton)** is a space observatory launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) in December 1999. Named in honor of Sir Isaac Newton, it is one of the largest scientific satellites ever built, carrying highly sensitive X-ray telescopes designed to detect radiation from some of the most energetic phenomena in the cosmos.

Key features of XMM-Newton include:

- **Exceptional collecting area**, thanks to its nested mirror modules, making it ideal for detecting faint X-ray sources
- **Simultaneous imaging and spectroscopy**, allowing detailed analysis of X-ray emitting objects
- **Long, uninterrupted observations** enabled by its highly elliptical orbit

## Studying Pulsars with XMM-Newton

The combination of pulsar science and XMM-Newton's capabilities has yielded remarkable discoveries. Because many pulsars emit significant portions of their energy in the X-ray band, XMM-Newton provides an invaluable window into their behavior. Researchers have used the observatory to:

- **Measure thermal emission** from the hot surfaces of neutron stars, offering clues about their internal structure and cooling processes
- **Detect non-thermal radiation** produced by particles accelerated in strong magnetic fields
- **Study pulsar wind nebulae**, the extended structures created when energetic particles interact with surrounding material
- **Constrain the equation of state** of ultra-dense matter, which remains one of physics' great unsolved problems

## Conclusion

The synergy between pulsar research and instruments like XMM-Newton continues to advance our knowledge of the universe's most extreme environments. Each observation brings us closer to understanding the fundamental nature of matter under conditions impossible to reproduce on Earth. As XMM-Newton continues its long and productive mission, it remains a cornerstone of high-energy astrophysics, illuminating the enigmatic lives of pulsars and other cosmic wonders.

# X-ray Detection of the Young Pulsar PSR J1357−6429 with XMM-Newton and Chandra

## Abstract

We report the first detection of X-ray emission from the young, energetic radio pulsar PSR J1357−6429 using observations obtained with the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories. With a characteristic age of ~7.3 kyr and a spin-down luminosity of Ė ≈ 3.1 × 10³⁶ erg s⁻¹, this pulsar is among the youngest and most energetic known in the Galaxy, yet had previously eluded detection at high energies. The Chandra data reveal a point source coincident with the radio pulsar position, embedded within diffuse emission suggestive of a compact pulsar wind nebula (PWN). The spectrum of the point source is well described by a composite model combining a thermal component, consistent with emission from the heated neutron star surface (kT ≈ 0.15 keV), and a non-thermal power-law component (photon index Γ ≈ 1.4–1.7) attributed to magnetospheric emission. The surrounding nebular emission exhibits a harder, purely non-thermal spectrum, consistent with synchrotron radiation from relativistic particles accelerated in the pulsar wind. Adopting a distance of 2.5 kpc, we derive an X-ray luminosity for the pulsar and nebula corresponding to an X-ray conversion efficiency of L_X/Ė ~ 10⁻³, in agreement with the trend established for other young, Vela-like pulsars. We discuss the implications of these results for the thermal evolution of the neutron star, the properties of its wind nebula, and the possible association of PSR J1357−6429 with the supernova remnant G309.8−2.6 and nearby TeV γ-ray sources. Our findings establish PSR J1357−6429 as a close analog to the Vela pulsar and a promising target for future multiwavelength and high-energy studies.

We discuss these results in the context of the evolutionary trends of young pulsars and their nebulae, and compare the source properties to other members of its class. # X-ray Properties of PSR J1357−6429

## Abstract

PSR J1357−6429 is a young, energetic radio pulsar (characteristic age τ ≈ 7.3 kyr, spin-down luminosity Ė ≈ 3.1 × 10³⁶ erg s⁻¹) located at an estimated distance of ~2.4 kpc. We present an analysis of its X-ray emission based on observations in the 0.5–10 keV band. The source spectrum is adequately described by an absorbed power-law model with a photon index of Γ ≈ 1.5–1.9, potentially supplemented by a thermal component consistent with emission from a cooling neutron star surface.

The inferred non-thermal X-ray luminosity yields an X-ray conversion efficiency of η = L_X/Ė ≈ 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁴, consistent with the empirical trend observed among rotation-powered pulsars of comparable age and spin-down power. This low efficiency indicates that only a small fraction of the pulsar's rotational energy loss is radiated in the X-ray regime.

A search for periodic modulation of the X-ray flux at the radio pulse period revealed no statistically significant pulsations. We place an upper limit on the pulsed fraction (modulation amplitude) of ≲30–50% (at the ~99% confidence level), constraining the geometry and beaming of the magnetospheric emission.

Extended emission attributable to a pulsar wind nebula (PWN) was investigated in the immediate vicinity of the pulsar. We derive an upper limit on the PWN X-ray luminosity, corresponding to an efficiency of L_PWN/Ė ≲ 10⁻³. This constraint suggests a comparatively faint or low-surface-brightness nebula relative to other young pulsars, with implications for the ambient density and the pulsar's evolutionary state.
